msDesc.head: A Persianate South Asian album of ten folios, with five paintings and drawings as well as five calligraphy specimens.

msContents.summary: This Persianate South Asian album of ten folios preserves five paintings and drawings, as well as five Persian calligraphy specimens. All folios bear the seal impression of Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), who served as Chief Justice in Calcutta between 1774 to 1783, during which time, he amassed a considerable collection of manuscripts, drawings, and antiquarian objects.

supportDesc.support: The first double-sided, appended leaf excepted, all folios appear prepared and uniformly mounted onto the same underlying heavy-weight paper, left blank.
supportDesc.condition: Handle with caution, Folios in fair condition, with abrasion and delamination along the for-edge. Margins smeared underneath Impey's seal impressions, perhaps to remove an earlier one.

physDesc.additions: Bookplates: The left pastedown: Bibliotheca Lindesiana with shelfmark 4/A, Bland MSS No. 75.

binding.p: Pamphlet-stitched through a three rectangular strips of paper. Case-bound in full, green silk striped brocade Endpapers of brilliant pink, early-19th century, coated wove paper. The same appears on Persian MS 51.
binding.condition: Handle with caution. Spine completed abraded away and delaminating from the front boards.

seal.p:
Rectangular seal impressions, intaglio carved in nasta‘līq script in two stacked lines, double-ruled, of former owner Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809), dated 1775, along with a regnal year 16 of George III, King of Great Britain (b. 1738, r. 1760–1820) reads from bottom upwards:
سر ایلاجه ایمپی چیف جستس سنه ۱۶، ۱۷۷۵
(Sir Īlāhah Īmpī Chīf Justis, sanah 16, 1775).
Dimensions:
19 26

history.origin: The content originates from different periods and sources, which an artist formed into an album either assembled for, or acquired by, Sir Elijah Impey (1732–1809) in Calcutta (Kolkata), as per his seal impressions. Impey served as the first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William between 1774 to 1783, where he amassed a considerable collection, before he returned to Britain and passed away.

provenance.p: The London firm of Harry Phillips (d. 1840) sold Impey's collection 21 May 1810, including five albums of ten folios, Nº 279–283.

Probably subsequently acquired by Methodist minister Rev. Adam Clarke (1762–1832), after whose death his son Jospeh Butterworth Bulmer Clarke (d. 1855) inherited the volume and describes its present state in a catalogue published in 1835.

The next year on 20 June 1836, Clarke's son auctioned his father's collection through the London firm of Sotheby & Son, Nº 147, where bookseller William Straker purchased it for £5 15 shillings and sixpence.
Probably sold by Straker to scholar Nathaniel Bland (1803–1865) for his library at Randalls Park, Leatherhead.

After Bland's death, London bookseller Bernard Quaritch (1819–1899) sold his oriental manuscripts to Alexander Lindsay, 25th Earl of Crawford (1812–1880) in June, 1866, paid in two instalments of £450 and £400, and then moved to Bibliotheca Lindesiana at Haigh Hall, Wigan.
Purchased by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1901 from James Ludovic Lindsay, 26th Earl of Crawford (1847–1913).

acquisition.p: Bequeathed by Enriqueta Rylands (1843–1908) in 1908 to the John Rylands Library, Manchester.

source.p: Bibliographical description based on a manuscript catalogue by Michael Kerney, circa 1890s.
Manuscript description by Jake Benson in 2026 with reference to the volume in hand.

msItem.quote: بازآی که از غم تو ما را * چشمی و هزار چشمه آب است | تندی و جفا و زشت‌خویی * هرچند که می‌کنی نکویی | فرمان برمت به هر چه گویی * جان بر لب و چشم بر خطاب است | ای روی تو از بهشت بابی * دل بر نمک لبت کبابی | گفتم بزنم بر آتش آبی * وین آتش دل نه جای آب است | ای سرو روان و گلبن نو * مه پیکرِ آفتاب‌پرتو | بستان و بده؛ بگوی و بشنو * شب‌های چنین نه وقت خواب است | این گُرسِنه‌گرگِ بی‌ترحم * خود سیر نمی‌شود ز مردم | ابنای زمان مثال گندم * وین دور فلک چو آسیاب است | سعدی تو نه مرد وصل اویی * تا لاف زنی و قرب جویی | از هرچه می‌رود، سخنِ دوست خوش‌تر است * پیغام آشنا، نفَسِ روح‌پرور است

msContents.summary: This calligraphy specimen primarily features a ghazal (lyric) poem with variant line order by ʻAbd al-Raḥman Jāmī (ca. 1414–1492), appended with a quatrain written vertically at right and left by an unidentified author. Unsigned and undated, it commences in the centre, then proceeds to the minuscule script the Hindu-Arabic number ۱۳ (13) appears at top, which suggests it derives from another album or manuscript. The style of sprayed stencil decoration suggests it may possibly be from the Safavid Empire in circa the 16th to 17th centuries CE.

msItem.quote: درین ره خضر همت همرهم بس * حریم نیستی منزلگهم بس | حریف کنج خلوتخانه فقر * دل هشیار و جان آگهم بس | چرا منت کشم بهر چراغی * فروغ مجلس از شمع مهم بس | مرا گر دولت شاهنشهی نیست * جگربسته درون خون ته تهم بس | ز بیرون گر لباس تو به تو نیست * فراغ از دولت شاهنشهم بس | چو جامی گر نه کوتاه آستینم * ز مشت سفله دست کوتهم بس
فریاد برآمد که گرفتاری چند * در زلف تو ای برده دلِ رازی چند | پرسیدم از نشان که گیاهند شما * دل‌ها دیدم بسته به هر تاری چند

msContents.summary: Safavid-era polymath Fatḥ Allāh Shīrāzī (d. ca. 1588) copied this excerpt from a ghazal (lyric) poem by Ḥāfiẓ (ca. 1315–1390) as a musaddis (sextain). Originally from Iran, the Deccan Sultanate rule ‘Alī ‘Ādil Shāh (r. 1558–1580) invited him to Bijapur, then after that patron's death, he received an invitation from the Mughal Emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605) to join his court in 1583, as an administrator, in which role he served admirably until his death in Kashmir five years later.

msContents.summary: Mughal-era court calligrapher, ‘Abd al-Raḥīm ‘Anbarīn Qalam ( fl. ca. 1580–1625) of Kashan, copied this excerpt from a ghazal (lyric) poem composed by Amīr Shāhī Sabzavārī, d. 1453 as a quatrain, in 986 AH (1578–1579 CE). When mounting this specimen, an artist pasted four fragments, two on blue paper at right and left inspired by lecture of ‘Abd Allāh Anṣārī (1006-1089), and two on orange-tinted paper at top and bottom, the latter signed Mushkīn Qalam, the siganture of Shaykh ʻAbd Allāh bin Mīr Muẓaffar al-Ḥusaynī al-Tirmiz̲ī (d. 1616 or 1626 CE), who also composed poetry under the pen name Vaṣfī.

msItem.title: Quatrain
msItem.author:
Hilālī, Badr al-Dīn, d. ca. 1528;
هلالى، بدر الدين
msItem.editor:
Shaykh ʻAbd Allāh bin Mīr Muẓaffar al-Ḥusaynī al-Tirmiz̲ī Mushkīn Qalam, Vaṣfī, d. 1616 or 1626 CE.;
شیخ عبدالله میر مظفر الحسینی الترمذی مشکین قلم
msItem.quote: آنی که تمام از نمکت ریخته‌اند * ذرات وجودت ز نمک بیخته‌اند | با شیرهٔ جان‌ها نمک آمیخته‌اند * تا همچو تو صورتی برانگیخته‌اند
از آنکه هر چه به من رسید ازو دیدم
کودکی و بستی جوانی و مستی* محرومست اگر برآب روی خسی
msItem.colophon: القیر عبد الله مشکین قلم غفر له
The poor ʻAbd Allāh Mushkīn Qalam forgive him.
msItem.note: For another anonymous quatrain and excerpt of a ghazal (lyric) poem by Ḥāfiẓ copied by ‘Abd al-Raḥīm Haravī ‘Anbarīn Qalam, see Indian Drawings 11, folio 22a and Indian Drawings 12, folio 32b respectively. For two works by ʻAbd Allāh Mushkīn Qalam held in the Rylands, see Persian MS 94 and Persian MS 297.
